commentary: The market's leadership flipped today, and that is the thing worth knowing. Money came out of the software and cybersecurity stocks that have led all year - Okta fell 4.5%, CrowdStrike 3.7%, Datadog 3.2% - and poured into the beaten-down chip names, with Micron up 12%, SanDisk 14%, Western Digital 13% and AMD 8%, lifting the S&P 0.9% on the day. The trigger was Morgan Stanley telling clients that memory chip prices should rise at least 25% next quarter and that the shortage runs into 2027 and 2028; that is exactly the evidence I said last week I needed before I could take Micron seriously as anything other than a cheap-looking cyclical. I still did not buy it, because I do not pay up the day after a 12% move in a stock that swings 8% on an average day - I have written down the two levels that would get me in instead. Two events decide the rest of this week: Alphabet and Tesla report Wednesday after the close, which is the first honest read on whether big tech is still spending on AI, and AMD holds its AI keynote Thursday morning. The book stays 100% in cash at $9,819, and the one risk I am not being paid for is the Iran war, which has crude up 6.6% in five sessions with a ceasefire proposal on the table that could reverse it just as fast.

** `market_news` reported fetching 119 items (yahoo 49, cnbc 30, marketwatch 10, alpaca 30) and surfaced **15**, and because the cap keeps the *most recent* headlines, all 15 were published in the final 30 minutes before the gather — four of them the identical "12 [Sector] Stocks Moving In Tuesday's After-Market Session" template. The result is that the entire macro narrative of the session was dropped: not one headline about the US–Iran strikes that have crude up 6.55% in five sessions, and consequently `market_events.flags.counts.geopolitical` scored **0** on a night with a ten-day ceasefire proposal live. A required regime input returned a confident false negative, and I only caught it because I ran outside web research. Two cheap fixes: (1) **stratify the headline cap** — reserve half the slots for market-wide/macro stories and half for single-name, instead of sorting purely by recency; (2) **collapse templated Benzinga movers lists** ("N [Sector] Stocks Moving In...") into one row before the cap, since they are structurally guaranteed to be the newest items every evening and currently crowd out everything that matters. Secondary, and cheaper still: nothing in the bundle told me *where* today's money went — `momentum_health` correctly flagged "unwind" but a one-line leadership-rotation read (top and bottom sectors by same-day move) would have handed me the single most important fact of this session instead of my having to reconstruct it from 186 individual `pct_change_1d` fields.

** The three ideas that actually competed for capital this run — UNH, TRV and MPC — are all *non-focus* names, so the bundle gave me a numeric scan row and nothing else: no candlestick chart, no options-implied expected move, no `stop_engineering` floor, no `ownership_flow`, no insider read. I had to judge UNH's entry geometry against a 200-week moving average I could not see on a chart, and I have no idea whether its options market is leaning the way GS's is. This is adopted lesson LP-8200625986 recurring verbatim, and today it was the *deciding* constraint rather than a nuisance: the scanner should promote the top 2–3 non-focus `top_setups` rows (or any name carrying a >5% 30-day upward EPS revision) into the focus set each run so they receive a chart plus the deep bundle. As it stands, the moment leadership rotates out of my 13 focus names — which is precisely what a momentum unwind *is* — my research depth rotates out with it.

** the watchlist trigger checker is **direction-blind**, and that is what produced this run's false positive. My published PANW condition was a *reclaim* of ~$345 that *holds*; the alert fired because price came within 2% of $345 **from below** (live $340.12, -2.45% on the day) — the opposite of the stated condition. This is the same class of defect as LP-4566902391 (the AMD alert firing 3.9% off the level). Fix: parse a relation token out of `would_buy_at` — "reclaim / above / breaks out / closes above" requires price **at or above** the level, "pullback to / near / dip to / below" requires price **at or below** — and only fire when the relation is satisfied, defaulting to proximity-only with an explicit `relation: unknown` tag when no token parses. Secondary, same block: the alert quoted PANW's stale 7/20 close ($348.66) while `live_prices.json`, written four minutes earlier, carried $340.12 — the alert rows should quote the same live mark the `trigger_run_note` claims to have confirmed on, or the two blocks will keep contradicting each other on exactly the days a trigger matters.

** The `holdings_watchlist` depth scanned exactly 10 names, and two of the twelve focus names — GS and KKR — arrived as tape/8-K promotions with *no scan row at all*: no ATR, no RSI, no trend labels, no chart, no anchored VWAP. GS carries the second-strongest 30-day EPS revisions in the entire universe screen (+18.75%) and `institutions_buying_price_weak`, and I had to shelve it purely because I could not place an honest stop or judge entry geometry. This is the same defect logged as LP-8200625986 on 2026-07-19 for MU, still unfixed: **tape/8-K promotions should inherit the full scan row (ATR, trend, volume signal, anchored VWAP) and a chart, not just news and fundamentals** — otherwise the promotion mechanism surfaces names it cannot let me underwrite, which is worse than not surfacing them. Second, smaller: my own CRWD trigger was conditioned on a confirmed MACD bull cross, an indicator this system's own 12-year study measured at −0.01pp. Nothing flagged the contradiction between a stored watchlist trigger and a knowledge-base finding that retired the indicator — a cheap check comparing trigger text against measured-dead indicators would have caught it a week ago.

** `momentum_health` was entirely absent from this bundle — no status, no MTUM/SPMO drawdown figures, no signals block — despite CLAUDE.md naming it as a required input to the regime step on *every* run, and this was precisely the week its answer mattered most. Worse, the failure is silent: the fail-open convention treats a missing block as "unknown, no adjustment," which is indistinguishable in the pack from a genuine `unknown` verdict on live data — so on a `weekly_market` depth the gather can drop the block entirely and nothing surfaces it. The fix is small: have the gatherer emit `momentum_health` on every depth (weekly included) and, when it genuinely cannot compute, emit an explicit `{"status": "unavailable", "reason": ...}` stub so the pack distinguishes "the factor is fine" from "nobody looked."

** The deterministic trigger check fired on AMD purely because the *price* touched the parsed $500 level, but my published `would_buy_at` was a compound condition — *post-event* confirmation plus a 50-DMA reclaim, explicitly excluding a pre-event dip. The result is a full event-driven run spun up for a setup that was never actually live, five days before its own catalyst. The trigger parser could be materially sharper if it also parsed an *event/date gate* from the trigger text (e.g. "after 7/22-23") and suppressed or down-weighted the alert until that date passes, rather than firing on the price alone. That would save event-driven runs for triggers whose *conditions*, not just prices, are met — reducing exactly this kind of "premature trigger" cycle.

** The single highest-value fix this run is upstream of my judgment: the orchestrator handed me a portfolio reading `$0 equity / $0 cash / no positions` with no `data_quality` or `stale_data_notice` flag raised, even though the trade history mathematically implies ~$9,820 should exist. A cheap deterministic guard — "if broker equity is ~$0 but closed-trade math implies non-trivial cash, flag `broker_sync_suspect` and set `allows_new_buys: false` with a reason" — would prevent a future run from being invited to trade (this was even a trigger-driven run) against an account it cannot possibly fund, and would save me from spending the cycle diagnosing broker plumbing instead of setups. Separately, the watchlist trigger checker should parse the *qualitative* half of `would_buy_at` (here, "confirmed positive reaction to the 7/22-23 event... not a bounce off today's low") rather than only the first dollar figure, so it stops firing event-driven runs on price alone before the event has occurred.

`gap_analysis` reports a gap's size, direction, and whether it later filled, but not how the session actually closed relative to its open — so UNH shows an unfilled +7.4% gap while `pct_change_1d` is only +1.16%, meaning most of the pop was sold intraday, and I had to infer that from two fields that don't reconcile on their face. A `close_vs_open_pct` (or an `intraday_fade` flag) on the gap object would let an evening review distinguish a *held* gap from a *faded* one, which is the entire difference between a real drift setup and a failed print — precisely the call I had to hedge on UNH tonight. Secondary: `momentum_health` was absent from this bundle entirely (not even `unknown`), and `position_histories` was `skipped`, so two documented inputs to the regime read were silently missing rather than explicitly null.

The relay bundle's intraday price for AMD (last_close $548.81, +2.7%) diverged meaningfully from independently-verified real-time coverage ($566.73, +6.05%) even though data_quality reported the bundle as only 0.5h old - on a day with a fast, catalyst-driven intraday move, a 0.5h-old snapshot for a non-focus scan name can already be stale enough to make a trigger look unconfirmed when live volume/price may have since caught up; worth having the gather step timestamp each ticker's price pull individually (not just the bundle as a whole) so I can weight staleness per-name rather than assuming uniform freshness across 50+ scanned tickers.

** For non-focus scan names that surface as genuine top candidates (MU this run — #2 EPS revision, cheapest-in-group, strong-buy), the bundle gives me the numeric row but withholds the chart, filing texts, options-implied move, and deep fundamentals I need to actually underwrite an entry — so a legitimately compelling name gets defaulted to the watchlist partly for lack of data rather than lack of merit. The scanner should promote the top 1–2 non-focus setups (by swing_setup_score or upward-revision rank) into the focus set each run so they receive a chart + deep bundle, letting me deep-research them the same cycle they appear instead of waiting a week.

** Two process gaps cost research time today. First, candlestick charts did not render this run — `data/charts/` was empty even though the gather log said "rendering candlestick charts..."; the chart step appears to depend on the same blocked live yfinance feed rather than falling back to the relay bundle the way the rest of the pipeline does, so I judged entry geometry on numeric indicators alone with no visual confirmation of the actual price bars. Second, the watchlist-trigger-alert logic flagged AMD as "price trigger reached" when the price was actually 3.9% away from my stated $555 level (outside the "within 2%" tolerance the note claims) — worth checking the matching logic, since a false trigger wastes a research pass and could eventually cause a bad entry if I trusted it without re-verifying, as I did here.

** The digest surfaced pre-classified insider signals (e.g. HOOD `insider_buying`, DELL `notable_discretionary_selling`), but my drill-down lookups on `insider_activity.by_ticker.<T>` returned null — the detail lives under `insider_activity.tickers.<T>.summary` instead, and I had to page through a 285KB raw transaction dump to confirm HOOD's buy was a single $55M discretionary buyer (one buyer, not a 2+ cluster). Exposing a compact per-ticker `signal + summary` object at the same key the digest points to — and echoing `distinct_discretionary_buyers` into the digest itself — would let me weight a contrarian insider-buying name like HOOD correctly without parsing the full Form-4 feed, saving research time for the names that matter.

Weekly self-review: This week was mostly build week, not trade week - the system went from a bare skeleton to a full pipeline (data relay, validator, position sizing, watchlist triggers, insider activity, sector relative strength, post-earnings drift detection) in a handful of commits, and only opened its first two live paper positions on 7/9 (DELL) and 7/10 (HPE). Neither has closed yet, so there is no win/loss to grade - the real test of the process comes next week when these mature past a few days and I have to apply the cash-test and thesis-break discipline for real, not just in theory. What I got right: discipline held under pressure - six separate runs today all correctly said no-trade rather than forcing a mediocre setup into a rate-driven, breadth-thin tape, and both live entries were valuation-anchored (12-20x forward earnings) rather than chases into the 40-170x names topping the momentum scan. What went wrong was mostly data quality, not reasoning: the insider Form-4 feed got flagged as noisy five separate times this week because financial-sponsor distributions (Silver Lake's Dell unwind, ALAB's post-lockup sales) bury genuine officer-conviction signals under hundreds of routine rows, a stale next_earnings field showed a past date for HPE, and the post_earnings_drift_candidate flag missed HPE's textbook drift setup because a one-time GAAP charge masked rising estimates - all bad data, not bad judgment, but they cost research time I'd rather spend on names. The one change for next week: get the insider feed pre-classified into sponsor/10b5-1 vs. discretionary officer transactions before it's handed to me, since that single fix has been the most repeated friction point of the week and is pure engineering, not agent judgment.

** The insider_activity feed is dominated by financial-sponsor unwinds (Silver Lake's programmatic Dell distribution ran to 79 separate line items) and routine 10b5-1 officer sales, which bury any genuinely informative *open-market* signal. A pre-computed classifier flag distinguishing "sponsor/PE distribution" and "scheduled 10b5-1" from "discretionary open-market officer buy/sell," plus a net cluster-buy score, would let me weight this data in seconds instead of scrolling hundreds of near-identical sell tickets to conclude "no signal."
